bp: The paper starts from a web that is no longer only a place where people click links, read pages, see ads, and subscribe to publications. It imagines a web where autonomous AI agents increasingly visit sites, collect information, summarize it, and act for users. That can make the web more useful: agents can automate search, comparison, form filling, and information gathering. But it also changes who receives value from online content. A newspaper may pay reporters, editors, and hosting bills, yet an agent can consume the article without delivering a human reader, an ad impression, or a subscription relationship. The paper asks how this new agent-mediated web can remain open and sustainable, especially from a Global South perspective. Its concern is not only whether agents can technically fetch content, but whether the rules of access, payment, and voice in governance let all affected groups keep participating.
wh: The hard part is that the same action can look useful to one actor and extractive to another. For an AI company or user, an agent reading web content is convenient automation. For a publisher, it may mean server costs, lost traffic, and weakened business models. For governments and civil society, it raises questions about who gets to set rules for the next web infrastructure. The abstract names three tensions: no standardized mechanisms for controlling AI-bot access to content, a mismatch between agent-based content consumption and current digital business models, and governance gaps that may amplify extractive dynamics. Blocking all bots is too crude because some automated access may be valuable. Legal disputes are too slow and fragmented to become daily infrastructure. The Global South perspective adds another difficulty: if rules are written mainly by powerful markets and firms, countries with less bargaining power may supply data and content without equal influence over benefits or protections.
naive: A smart beginner might say: just block unwanted bots with site rules, and sue the companies that ignore them. That sounds direct, but the abstract treats current broad bot blocking and legal disputes as symptoms of a deeper misalignment. Blocking is blunt because it can keep out useful agents along with harmful ones, and it does not create a shared price, permission, or accountability system. Lawsuits can punish particular behavior, but they do not tell every publisher, platform, agent builder, and user how ordinary access should work tomorrow. Another naive answer is to let the market decide, but that favors actors who already control technical infrastructure, user traffic, and capital.
ap: The paper's core idea is to shift the question from bot control to incentive alignment. Instead of asking only how a website can stop or allow an AI crawler, it asks what economic and governance mechanisms would make cooperation rational for publishers, agent developers, platforms, governments, and users. The evidence base is a multi-stakeholder workshop in Brazil with 28 representatives from major technology companies, media groups, newspapers, academia, and government. From that discussion, the authors identify a pattern: access rules, business models, and governance voice are being handled separately even though they affect one another. Their proposed direction is transparent standards for access, inclusive governance so Global South actors help shape rules, and multi-stakeholder coordination to rebalance incentives. In concrete terms, the paper argues that the agentic web needs shared mechanisms for permission, compensation, and accountability, not just isolated technical blocks or court fights.
mech: The input to this position paper is not a dataset of clicks or model outputs. It is a set of stakeholder observations gathered through the Brazil workshop, plus the visible change in web behavior as AI agents mediate more content consumption. The paper first names the actors: technology companies building agents, media organizations and newspapers producing content, academic experts, government representatives, and the communities affected by the resulting infrastructure. It then sorts the problem into three linked mechanisms. The access mechanism asks how a content owner can communicate what AI-bots may do and how those instructions are recognized. The economic mechanism asks how value moves when an agent consumes content without producing the same traffic, advertising, or subscription events that human browsing produced. The governance mechanism asks who has standing to set and enforce rules, especially when Global South institutions may otherwise be rule-takers. The paper compares current responses against these mechanisms. Broad blocking may express refusal, but it does not distinguish acceptable from unacceptable access. Legal disputes may establish pressure, but they do not create an everyday coordination layer. The output is an argument for rebalanced infrastructure: transparent standards, inclusive decision-making, and coordinated agreements that let agents access content under rules that content producers and affected societies can understand and contest.
math: The relevant mathematics is not a new predictive model; it is the logic of incentives, coordination, and mechanism design. Mechanism design means arranging rules so that each participant's locally sensible choice also supports the shared system. In plain terms, if publishers earn nothing when agents reuse their work, their sensible move is to block. If agent builders face no cost for extraction, their sensible move is to take as much as possible. The system then moves toward conflict even if everyone would benefit from a healthier web. Incentive alignment asks what payments, permissions, disclosures, or enforcement rules would make cooperation more attractive than defection. Game-theoretic reasoning is the everyday idea that each actor chooses while anticipating what others will do: publishers anticipate crawlers, crawlers anticipate blocks, governments anticipate market power, and users anticipate service quality. Standards are coordination devices. They reduce uncertainty by giving many parties a common language for allowed access. The tradeoff is openness versus control: too much control fragments the web, while too little control lets powerful agents extract value from weaker content producers. The Global South lens matters because bargaining power is uneven, so a formally open rule can still produce unequal outcomes if rule-making power is concentrated.
dots: This paper belongs near the conference's agent and tool-use work, but it asks the governance question beneath those systems. Many agent papers ask how an AI system can browse, retrieve, compare, or act more effectively. This paper asks what happens to the web's producers and institutions when that behavior becomes normal. It also connects to matching and allocation: the local math file for gid 288 tags it as designing rules so agents, publishers, platforms, and advertisers have incentives to cooperate instead of blocking or suing. The neighboring batch reinforces the broader theme of AI reshaping web trust and safety: fake-news detection, AI safety workshops, and medical QA safety all ask what must be controlled before automation is trusted. Here the controlled object is not a model's answer but access to content and value flows. The paper also connects to fairness and responsible AI because the Global South perspective asks whether governance includes those who may otherwise be mined for data, content, and labor without equal bargaining power.
ww: The proposal works, if it works, because the current conflict is not caused by one missing software switch. It comes from mismatched incentives. A publisher asked to subsidize agent access with no traffic or payment has a reason to refuse. An agent builder facing fragmented rules has a reason to crawl wherever it can. Governments and civil groups left out of rule-making have a reason to distrust the infrastructure. Transparent standards can reduce ambiguity: agents can know what is allowed, publishers can express permissions in a common way, and disputes can refer to shared expectations. Inclusive governance can reduce extraction by giving Global South stakeholders a seat before rules harden into defaults. Multi-stakeholder coordination can connect the technical layer to the economic layer, so access is tied to compensation, accountability, or negotiated permission. That is stronger than the naive approach because it changes the repeated choices actors face. Instead of making every interaction a private fight between crawler and website, it tries to create a shared environment where cooperation is less costly than conflict.
po: The payoff is a practical reframing of the Agentic Web as an infrastructure problem rather than only a crawling problem. The paper identifies three central tensions and argues that blocking and litigation alone cannot solve them. Its contribution is a Global South situated agenda for transparent standards, inclusive governance, and incentive rebalancing. If adopted, those mechanisms could let useful agents operate while giving publishers and affected societies clearer control over access, value, and accountability. The result would be a more sustainable open web, not simply a web where the strongest actors automate extraction fastest.
limits: The abstract describes a position paper based on a 28-person workshop, so it should not be read as proof that one policy design will work globally. The argument depends on the workshop capturing important stakeholder concerns, but it cannot represent every publisher, country, language community, user, or agent builder. It also names directions rather than specifying a complete standard, payment rule, enforcement process, or governance institution. For the proposal to work, powerful technology companies would need reasons to accept shared rules, and Global South participation would need real authority rather than symbolic consultation. The abstract does not prove how conflicts between openness, compensation, and national regulation should be resolved.
